title: Linked-list walk idioms
description: The three boilerplate walks every LL problem uses: single walk, parallel walk, and dummy-head builder.

conversation.intro: This is a syntax-template lesson — three almost-identical linked-list loops. The interview script focuses on which template fits which job and the small idioms that prevent off-by-one bugs. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. When do you reach for each walk?
sections.say:
"Three linked-list loop shapes, three jobs:

• SINGLE WALK — `let curr = head; while (curr) { ...; curr = curr.next; }`. Use for any one-list operation: count, search, find-Nth, reverse, sum, print. The loop guard `while (curr)` terminates safely on null and handles the empty list without a special case.

• PARALLEL WALK — `let a = h1, b = h2; while (a && b) { ...; a = a.next; b = b.next; }`. Use for two-list operations: merge, compare, intersection, zip. The `&&` stops the loop the instant either list runs out, then you handle the remainder afterward.

• DUMMY-HEAD BUILDER — `const dummy = { val: 0, next: null }; let tail = dummy; while (...) { tail.next = newNode; tail = tail.next; } return dummy.next;`. Use whenever you're CONSTRUCTING a new list. The sentinel removes the 'is this the first node?' branch — you always just do `tail.next = newNode`.

Most real LL problems combine two of these: e.g. 'merge two sorted lists' = parallel walk + dummy-head builder. 'Reverse list' = single walk with a three-pointer dance. 'Add two numbers' = parallel walk + dummy-head builder + carry."
sections.why: Naming the three templates as templates — and pointing out that real problems COMPOSE them — is the fluency move. Most candidates write the loop fresh for each problem; the candidate who's drilled the family writes 'OK, this is parallel walk + dummy-head builder' and the code falls out in 30 seconds. Interviewers grade on that recognition speed.

sections.title: 2. Why these shapes, not other loop forms?
sections.say:
"Why `while (curr)` instead of `while (curr.next)`? Because the second form skips the LAST node and crashes if `head` is null. `while (curr)` walks all the way to null and terminates cleanly — handles the empty list `head === null` without a special case, because the loop just never enters.

Why `while (a && b)` for the parallel walk? Because the moment EITHER list runs out, you should stop the lockstep advance. If you wrote `while (a || b)` you'd dereference null on whichever ran out first. The standard pattern is: stop the lockstep on `&&`, then handle the leftover with `tail.next = a || b` outside the loop.

Why the dummy sentinel? Without it, the first append is a special case — `if (!head) head = newNode; else tail.next = newNode`. With the sentinel, the first append is `tail.next = newNode` just like every subsequent one. One branch removed, one source of off-by-one removed."
sections.why: Defending the loop guards is the fluency signal — anyone who's debugged a linked-list problem has hit the 'while (curr.next) skips the last node' bug or the 'first-node special case' bug. Calling out WHY each guard is shaped the way it is shows you've earned the boilerplate, not memorized it. The 'tail.next = a || b' trick for the leftover is the senior touch — most candidates write an `if (a) tail.next = a; else tail.next = b;` block that's correct but bulky.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern: combining two templates
sections.prompt: How real problems compose the building blocks.
sections.say:
"When you read a new LL problem, decompose it into the building blocks:

• Need to read ONE list and produce a scalar (count, sum, find) → SINGLE WALK.
• Need to read ONE list and BUILD a new list (copy, double, filter) → SINGLE WALK + DUMMY-HEAD BUILDER.
• Need to read TWO lists and produce a scalar (compare, intersect) → PARALLEL WALK.
• Need to read TWO lists and BUILD a new list (merge, zip, add two numbers) → PARALLEL WALK + DUMMY-HEAD BUILDER.
• Need to MUTATE in place (reverse, swap pairs, remove duplicates) → SINGLE WALK with extra pointers (prev/next) cached per iteration.

The L3 prompt for this lesson — `doubleList` — is the 'single walk + dummy-head builder' shape: walk the input with `curr = curr.next`, and on each step attach a brand-new `{val: curr.val * 2, next: null}` to the builder's tail."
sections.why: Decomposing problems into the building blocks BEFORE writing code is the move that prevents 'where do I start?' freezes. Once you've named 'this is parallel walk + dummy-head builder', the structure is forced — you write the scaffold first, then fill in the per-iteration logic. Interviewers love this because the candidate doesn't have to think; they just instantiate.

sections.title: 4. Trace through a tiny example
sections.prompt: Walk the L3 doubleList canonical (single-walk + dummy-head builder) on a small input.
sections.intro: "Let me trace `doubleList([1,2,3])` to make sure the dummy-head builder is doing what I think."

examples.note: Standard case — single walk reads input nodes, dummy-head builder constructs the output.
examples.trace:
init: dummy={val:0,next:null}, tail=dummy, curr=node(1)
iter1: tail.next={val:2}, tail=node(2), curr=node(2)  → builtSoFar=[2]
iter2: tail.next={val:4}, tail=node(4), curr=node(3)  → builtSoFar=[2,4]
iter3: tail.next={val:6}, tail=node(6), curr=null     → builtSoFar=[2,4,6]
loop exits (curr=null), return dummy.next = node(2) → [2,4,6]

examples.note: Empty input — single walk never enters, dummy.next stays null, return null → empty list.
examples.trace:
init: dummy={val:0,next:null}, tail=dummy, curr=null
loop check: curr is null → never enter
return dummy.next = null → []

examples.note: Single node — one iteration of the builder. Confirms there's no first-node special case.
examples.trace:
init: dummy={val:0,next:null}, tail=dummy, curr=node(42)
iter1: tail.next={val:84}, tail=node(84), curr=null  → builtSoFar=[84]
loop exits, return dummy.next = node(84) → [84]

sections.why: Tracing the empty-input case is the move — `while (curr)` returning immediately means the empty list works WITHOUT a `if (head === null) return null` guard. That's the whole point of the loop guard shape. Tracing single-node confirms there's no first-node special case in the builder either — the sentinel pattern means iteration 1 is mechanically the same as iteration N.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & pitfalls
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Pitfalls when you drop these templates into a real problem:
• Empty list (head = null) → `while (curr)` skips the loop, returns the right default (0 for count, null/empty for builder). ✓ No special case needed.
• Single node → loop runs exactly once, then `curr.next` is null and the loop exits. ✓
• Forgetting to advance `tail = tail.next` after `tail.next = newNode` → you overwrite the same slot every iteration and the builder produces a 1-node list. Classic off-by-one.
• Returning `dummy` instead of `dummy.next` → the sentinel itself leaks into the output, with `val: 0` (or whatever placeholder) at the front. Always `return dummy.next`.
• Parallel walk: forgetting to attach the remainder (`tail.next = a || b`) after the `while (a && b)` loop — the longer list's tail gets dropped silently.
• Using `while (curr.next)` instead of `while (curr)` for a single walk — skips the last node, crashes on empty.
• Mutating the input list when the problem expects an immutable read — always read into a copy if the contract is unclear.
• Cycle in the input → `while (curr)` never terminates. Worth flagging that the single walk assumes acyclic input; if cycles are possible, use Floyd's detection first or cap iterations."
sections.why: The 'forgetting to advance tail' bug is the canonical builder gotcha — every junior writes it once. Naming it before you write the code is cheap insurance. The 'return dummy not dummy.next' bug is the other classic — the sentinel pattern is great until you forget the sentinel itself isn't part of the output. The cycle-detection callout is the senior touch: most candidates assume acyclic silently, and an interviewer either nods or says 'assume acyclic for now' — both fine.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & common follow-ups
sections.prompt: What do these templates cost, and what problems use them?
sections.say:
"Each template is O(n) time and O(1) extra space if you're walking in place; O(n) extra space if you're building a new list via the dummy-head builder (one node per input node). Per-iteration work is constant — one pointer dereference, one pointer assignment, optionally one node allocation. No nested loops, no amortization argument needed.

Common follow-ups that use one or more of these templates as the SKELETON:
• SINGLE WALK → Count nodes, Find Middle (with fast/slow), Linked List Cycle (with fast/slow), Remove Nth From End, Reverse Linked List (single walk + 3-pointer dance), Palindrome Linked List.
• PARALLEL WALK → Merge Two Sorted Lists, Add Two Numbers, Intersection of Two Linked Lists, Compare Lists.
• DUMMY-HEAD BUILDER → Merge Two Sorted Lists, Remove Duplicates From Sorted List, Partition List, Remove Linked List Elements, Add Two Numbers (carry-as-you-build).

When you see ANY of those, the first thing on the whiteboard is one of these three templates."
sections.why: Listing the follow-up family for each template is what shows you see them as REUSABLE PRIMITIVES, not standalone tricks. The 'first thing on the whiteboard' phrasing also signals fluency — you're not deriving these per-problem, you're instantiating known boilerplate. Interviewers love this because it means the candidate will pattern-match the next LL problem instead of solving from scratch.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the canonical `doubleList(head)` — the L3 of this lesson — which combines a single walk on the input with the dummy-head builder pattern. Watch curr advance one node per step while tail and dummy.next grow on the output side.
trace: const toArr = (n) => { const out = []; while (n) { out.push(n.val); n = n.next; } return out; };
const dummyIn = { val: null, next: null };
for (const v of input) { tailIn.next = { val: v, next: null }; tailIn = tailIn.next; }
yield { line: 1, label: `enter doubleList — input list ${JSON.stringify(input)}`, state: { input, list: toArr(head) } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'create dummy sentinel { val:0, next:null } — eliminates first-node special case', state: { input, list: toArr(head), dummy: dummy.val, built: [] } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init tail = dummy (builder pointer starts at sentinel)', state: { input, list: toArr(head), built: [] } };
yield { line: 4, label: `init curr = head (= ${curr ? curr.val : 'null'}) — input walker`, state: { input, remaining: toArr(curr), curr: curr ? curr.val : null, built: [] } };
yield { line: 5, label: `loop entry iter ${iter} — curr=${curr.val}, will create new node with val=${curr.val * 2}`, state: { remaining: toArr(curr), curr: curr.val, built: toArr(dummy.next) } };
yield { line: 6, label: `tail.next = { val: ${curr.val * 2} } — attach new node to builder`, state: { remaining: toArr(curr), curr: curr.val, built: toArr(dummy.next), tailVal: tail.val } };
yield { line: 7, label: `tail = tail.next — advance builder pointer to ${tail.val}`, state: { remaining: toArr(curr), curr: curr.val, built: toArr(dummy.next), tailVal: tail.val } };

yield { line: 8, label: `curr = curr.next → ${curr ? curr.val : 'null'} (advance input walker)`, state: { remaining: toArr(curr), curr: curr ? curr.val : null, built: toArr(dummy.next), tailVal: tail.val } };
yield { line: 10, label: `loop done — return dummy.next (skip sentinel) → ${JSON.stringify(result)}`, state: { built: result, returns: JSON.stringify(result) } };

notes: Single walk: while(curr) terminates safely on null — no need to test curr.next.
Parallel walk uses && so the loop stops the moment either list runs out; attach the remainder afterwards.
Dummy head is a sentinel — it eliminates the 'is this the first node?' branch and lets you always do tail.next = ....
Always advance tail = tail.next after attaching, or you'll overwrite the same slot next iteration.

questions.q: Which loop condition safely walks a single linked list to the end?
questions.explain: while(curr) terminates cleanly when curr becomes null; while(curr.next) would skip the last node and throw if head is null.

questions.q: What does a dummy-head sentinel buy you when building a new list?
options: Lets you return the head pointer without walking back through the list
Removes the special case for inserting the first node
Reduces traversal cost from O(n) to O(n/2) by skipping the sentinel slot
Lets you delete from the front of the list in O(1) without losing the head reference
questions.explain: With a sentinel you can always do tail.next = newNode without branching on 'is this the very first append?'.

questions.q: When do you reach for the parallel walk `while (a && b)`?
options: Reversing a single list in place
Comparing or merging two lists in lockstep
Detecting a cycle in one list
questions.explain: Parallel walk is for two-list problems — merge, compare, intersection — where you advance both pointers each iteration.

questions.q: After building a list with a dummy head, what do you return?
questions.explain: dummy is the sentinel; the real list starts at dummy.next.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the single-walk loop that counts nodes in a list.
Fill in the dummy-head builder that copies values from an array into a new list.
Fill in the parallel walk that returns true only if every paired value is equal (stops the moment either list runs out).

blanks.hint: loop only while BOTH are non-null

L3.prompt: Write `doubleList(head)` that returns a NEW list with each value doubled, using the dummy-head builder. Log `JSON.stringify(toArr(doubleList(toList([1, 2, 3]))))`.
hints: Combine single walk (curr = curr.next) with the dummy-head builder.
Attach a brand-new node each step; return dummy.next, not dummy.
